reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of transaldolase (TALDO1 gene) in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway, leading to accumulation of polyols and seven-carbon sugars
Often presents in the neonatal or antenatal period with hepatosplenomegaly, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia, sometimes with hydrops
A multisystem disorder that can include dysmorphic features, cutis laxa or skin changes, cardiac and renal anomalies, and anaemia
Urine polyol analysis shows elevated erythritol, arabitol and ribitol, and characteristic seven-carbon sugars such as sedoheptulose and its derivatives
Progressive liver disease with fibrosis or cirrhosis is a major feature, and hepatocellular carcinoma has been reported
There is no specific enzyme-replacement therapy, so management is supportive with monitoring of hepatic, renal, haematological and cardiac function, and antioxidant approaches have been explored
Diagnosis relies on the urinary polyol/sugar pattern with confirmatory TALDO1 molecular testing
reference.pathophysiology: Transaldolase catalyses a reversible step in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway that interconverts sugar phosphates and links the pathway with glycolysis. Its deficiency disrupts the balance of pentose phosphate intermediates, causing accumulation of polyols (such as erythritol, arabitol and ribitol) and seven-carbon sugars (including sedoheptulose). The disturbed pathway is thought to increase oxidative stress and impair regeneration of reducing equivalents, contributing to progressive injury of the liver, kidneys, heart and blood cells. The result is a multisystem disorder dominated by hepatosplenomegaly, hepatic fibrosis, coagulopathy and cytopenias, often evident from birth.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal haemochromatosis and other neonatal liver failure syndromes
Other pentose phosphate pathway defects (ribose-5-phosphate isomerase deficiency)
Cutis laxa syndromes with systemic involvement
Tyrosinaemia type I and other metabolic liver diseases
additionalInvestigations: Urine polyol analysis for erythritol, arabitol and ribitol
Urine and body-fluid sugar analysis for sedoheptulose and seven-carbon sugar derivatives
Liver function tests, coagulation profile and full blood count
Abdominal imaging to assess hepatosplenomegaly and hepatic architecture
Renal and cardiac assessment for associated anomalies
TALDO1 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Neonatal liver failure with coagulopathy or bleeding
Hydrops fetalis or severe antenatal hepatosplenomegaly
Progressive hepatic fibrosis or signs suggesting hepatocellular carcinoma
Multisystem deterioration with cardiac or renal failure
reference.prognosis: The disorder is variable but often serious, with progressive liver disease, coagulopathy and multisystem involvement; some individuals survive into later childhood or adulthood while others succumb to neonatal liver failure or complications such as hepatocellular carcinoma.
pitfalls: Overlooking transaldolase deficiency in neonatal liver failure by not requesting urinary polyol analysis
Attributing hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias solely to congenital infection
Failing to monitor for evolving hepatic fibrosis and hepatocellular carcinoma over time
Missing associated renal, cardiac or dysmorphic features that point to a multisystem metabolic disorder
references: Scriver's OMMBID: Disorders of the Pentose Phosphate Pathway
Saudubray, Baumgartner & Walter, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
